rows: Celsius positioned as 'Energy 2.0' competing directly with Red Bull and Monster, riding a five-to-ten-year health-and-wellness movement.
Cleaner label (no sugar, no artificial preservatives/colors/flavors, seven essential vitamins) and fitness-rooted authenticity drive resonance.
PepsiCo partnership (signed Aug 1, 2022, 8.5% stake; distribution transitioned Oct 1, 2022) lifted ACV from ~65% to ~95%.
Over 80% of consumption is incremental to the category - retailers value new dollars, not trade-out from Red Bull/Monster.
Demographics differ from traditional energy: ~50-50 male/female, over-indexing female/African-American/Hispanic; 18-24 the fastest-growing segment.
SKU/facing gap remains large: ~15 SKUs per location vs ~25 for peers, who also have 40-50 facings and multi-shelf 'super SKUs.'
Negotiating 2024 shelf space from a ~10 share #3 position vs a ~3.5 share a year ago - should drive more SKUs, better placement, trial.
South Florida share rose from ~17.7% to ~24% in 10 months - the drill-deep playbook to be replicated across 30 markets in 2024.
Convenience is 58% of sales vs ~70% for Monster/Red Bull - meaningful channel headroom; Circle K divisions still ramping.
Food service a major new unlock via Pepsi - Jersey Mike's (~2,000 locations) a proof-of-concept; Pepsi caters to ~60% of the US college population.
Capturing college-age heavy users (one-to-two cans/day) could solidify lifetime consumers with a 50-60 year runway.
Operations led by ex-Monster global ops head Paul Story; 'orbit strategy' (up to eight orbits) minimizes miles on product; ~2 billion cans in 2023.
Promotional focus is depth (e.g., two-for-$4 vs two-for-$4.50) to capture margin; energy category promoted ~25 weeks/year.
Celsius priced between Red Bull and Monster; if Red Bull's price nears $4/can, that becomes an opportunity to capture trade-down consumers.
Celsius runs retailer exclusives over a period rather than short-lived LTOs - rewards partners and earns reciprocity.
A 250ml lower-caffeine offering is under consideration (TBD); new core and Vibe flavors coming in 2024; discipline on not launching too much at once.
Branded coolers a 'silent salesman' - pay for themselves in 4-6 months (~three days at a Walmart); ~20,000 placed in 2023; amortized over 5-7 years.
Tracked-channel scan data understates true performance - ~$250M untracked Costco/Amazon run rate distorts velocity/share; gap should narrow in 1-2 years.
Amazon (#1) and Instacart (#1) are 'neutral playing fields' lacking competitors' shelf advantage - proof points for brick-and-mortar potential.
~$750M cash earns interest offsetting the Pepsi dividend; M&A and vertical integration are 'on the table' but approached cautiously.
Q3 gross margin >50% included one-off benefits; ~49% normalized / the Q2 profile is the near-term baseline; ~55% gross / 30-35% EBITDA aspirational.
Aspirational ~55% gross margin equates to Monster's ~59% three years ago, adjusted for a ~4% outbound-freight classification delta.
Digital-first marketing ('own the phone') via targeted ads (Hulu, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat) drives precise targeting and ROI visibility.
International methodical: Canada launch Q1 2024 with Pepsi Canada; evaluating Europe, Japan, Australia; build framework, then expand faster in 2025-2026; US remains the priority.
What about the Celsius product resonates so much with consumers to support the rapid growth.

Celsius capitalizes on a five-to-ten-year health-and-wellness movement; born in 2005 as a pre-workout supplement, now a multi-occasion energy beverage with a cleaner label and fitness-rooted authenticity - 'Energy 2.0' competing with Red Bull and Monster. Demographics differ from traditional energy (24-45, with 18-24 the fastest-growing segment, balanced male/female) - driving share from outside traditional energy.
How the Pepsi distribution partnership fueled growth and the incremental opportunity it brings.

The deal (signed Aug 1, 2022, Pepsi taking an 8.5% stake; distribution transitioned Oct 1, 2022) lifted ACV from ~65% to ~90% by year-end and ~95% now. Pepsi is best-in-class in distribution/merchandising; velocities maintained despite the massive distribution gain; food service is a major new unlock. Celsius aims to be the #1 energy drink in Pepsi's portfolio.
The opportunity to increase available SKUs and facings, especially relative to Monster and Red Bull.

Celsius is at ~15 SKUs per location vs ~25 for peers, who also have far more facings (40-50, with multi-shelf 'super SKUs'). Celsius is mostly one SKU/one facing - opportunity for more SKUs, more facings, better locations. Negotiated 2024 shelf space from a ~10 share #3 position vs a ~3.5 share a year earlier, which should drive trial and stickiness.
Reaching beyond the core energy consumer
How Celsius's unique characteristics enhance its ability to reach beyond the core energy consumer and gain shelf space outside traditional energy positions.

Celsius brings new consumers - over 80% of consumption incremental (44% new-to-category, ~40% user intensification) - which retailers value as new dollars. Higher ring rate merits more space; over-indexes with females (~50-50 split), African-American, Hispanic and college-age consumers, while also appealing to people in their 50s-60s.
What allows Celsius to win with white-collar office workers, atypical for energy drinks.

Celsius's cleaner-label perception and fitness roots give it a different reputation - someone arriving at the office with a Celsius is not perceived as hungover, unlike with more aggressive brands. Framed almost as a 'functional soda' with multiple usage occasions (replacing morning/afternoon coffee, paired with lunch).
Whether share is gained from new consumers or from competitors, and how markets are expanded.

Celsius wants both - new consumers and pulling from Monster/Red Bull (~70-75% of the category). Cited Amazon (#1, having passed Monster) and South Florida (~24% share, up from ~17.7%) as proof points. Drill-deep started with five markets plus New York; resourced markets expanded from 18 (2022) to 23 (2023) to 30 (2024). Convenience is 58% of sales vs ~70% for peers - room to grow.
How long it takes to mature a new market.

It should not take 10 years like South Florida; each market is unique, needing a toggled playbook for regionality/culture. Declined a firm timeline but noted South Florida jumped 17.7% to 24% in 10 months; anticipates market-share gains in newer markets. Brand awareness in newer markets is relatively low after only 12-24 months of focus.
Which markets Celsius is in and their energy-drink ranking.

Drill-deep markets are top-10 energy markets; L.A. the largest, Dallas #2-3, Miami top-10, Tampa top-25, New England top-20, New York top-5 - an '80-20 rule' of large metros driving energy sales. With ~$300M revenue at ~20% S&M, Celsius has ~$300M vs $150M of marketing capital to accelerate markets.
About operations leadership, co-packing capacity and vertical integration.

Hired ex-Monster global ops head Paul Story ~2.5 years ago. Plenty of capacity; works with the biggest can companies (Ball, Crown, Ardagh); ~13 co-packers; an 'orbit strategy' with up to eight orbits minimizes miles on product. All co-packed today; vertical integration could be considered if it makes sense (Monster's flavor-house acquisition cited as precedent).
Color on the recently announced Dunkin' and Jersey Mike's wins and the food-service opportunity with Pepsi.

Pepsi's bandwidth opened food service; Pepsi CEO Ramon Laguarta helped bring a retired Pepsi food-service executive onto Celsius's team. Jersey Mike's (~2,000 locations) is a proof-of-concept for other Pepsi-oriented eateries. The college/university component is huge - Pepsi caters to ~60% of the US college population - giving access to early-adopter heavy consumers.
Whether capturing a consumer at the college level could solidify a lifetime Celsius consumer as they enter the workforce.

Theoretically that is the goal - retaining consumers as long as possible, with a potential 50-60 year runway. The 18-25 crowd are heavy users (one-to-two cans/day), so getting in early matters, as does the blue-collar consumer. Celsius can capture people for a decade or 15 years, similar to Red Bull/Monster.
Whether there is ample co-manufacturing capacity to scale up given strong growth.

Very confident it can produce as it scales - will sell close to 2 billion cans in 2023 - and can flex with different co-packers (~13 total, predominantly 6-7 used), including Refresco, which has multiple domestic and global locations for international expansion.
What Celsius is seeing in promotional spend and what retail partners expect on promotion and pricing.

The energy category is highly promoted (~25 weeks/year); focus is promotional depth (two-for-$4 vs two-for-$4.50) to capture margin without losing sales. Red Bull is 'supposedly' taking price - question of whether it deals down on promotion. Celsius makes pricing decisions largely independent of competitors, having taken price in early 2022 ahead of others.
How Celsius thinks about its price position relative to competition and whether maintaining a price gap matters.

Celsius is priced between Red Bull and Monster (more expensive per ounce but in between on shelf price); believes it has price elasticity. As a growth brand, if Red Bull's price nears $4/can, that becomes an opportunity to capture Red Bull consumers trading down to Celsius at ~$2.75-$3. A small team meets monthly to review analytics; the consumer views Celsius as premium.
What role limited-time and seasonal offerings play in the merchandising strategy and what to expect entering the new year.

Celsius historically does not do short-lived LTOs/seasonals; instead it runs retailer exclusives over a period (7-Eleven green apple cherry exclusive all of 2023, rolling national in January 2024; the 16oz Essentials line launched early at 7-Eleven with a two-month four-SKU exclusivity, rolling nationwide January 2024). Exclusivity is part of taking care of retail partners.
About new product formats / lower-caffeine offerings.

A 250ml (Red Bull-can-style) lower-caffeine offering could make sense but no decisions made ('TBD'). With the 16oz line just rolled out, management does not want to launch too much at once; new core and Vibe flavors are also coming in 2024. A lower-caffeine version could capture an extra daily occasion (e.g., 4:00 p.m.).
The opportunity in expanding branded fridge placements and whether they drive incremental trial.

Cooler sales are 'astronomical' in good positions; coolers pay for themselves in 4-6 months (~three days at a well-positioned Walmart). CEO called out a push for ~20,000 total coolers placed in 2023. Coolers are a 'silent salesman' providing incremental placement; amortized over 5-7 years.
Whether retailers push back on fridge placements.

Depends on the retailer; placements happen where Celsius or Pepsi has a relationship with the owner/manager. Celsius previously offered 'free fill' but rarely needs to now because stores see the incremental dollar value. Some retailers (e.g., 7-Eleven) do not allow branded coolers; independent convenience and Walmart/Target are key opportunities.
About the commodity basket and how management feels about gross margins moving into 2024.

Gross margins improved over the prior 12 months - Q3 came in just over 50% (with one-off benefits; ~49% normalized) and the Q2 profile is the near-term baseline. Monster is the long-term benchmark, adjusting for Monster excluding outbound freight from COGS (~4% delta) - Monster's ~59% three years ago equates to ~55% for Celsius (aspirational, achievable with scale and possible vertical integration). EBITDA margin ~27% vs a 30-35% target.
Whether the ~$750M cash just builds or there are key deployment opportunities.

The ~$750M earns interest that offsets the Pepsi dividend, giving flexibility for M&A. Management will be strategic - the priority is the core 'unicorn' brand and driving share; M&A and vertical integration are 'on the table' but approached cautiously and must make sense to investors.
Sales & marketing spend and acquisition costs
About sales and marketing spend levels and customer acquisition.

S&M as a percentage of revenue will continue at a similar rate - recently ~19%, ~21-22% prior, likely somewhere in between. The marketing mantra is 'own the phone' via targeted digital ads (Hulu, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat), enabling precise targeting and better ROI visibility, especially driving to Amazon/Walmart for immediate sales.
About the gap between tracked-channel data and reported results.

The tracked-vs-reported gap should narrow in a year or two. Much remaining opportunity is in independent non-tracked channels owned by Red Bull/Monster. Celsius generates ~$250M run rate (~$500M retail) from untracked Costco and Amazon, distorting tracked velocity/share comparisons. Celsius is #1 on Amazon and #1 on Instacart; disclosing South Florida data drew 50-100 competitor reps into the market.
Whether there is anything different about the Amazon #1 customer.

Pretty much everyone uses Amazon - a 'neutral playing field' where Red Bull and Monster lack their multi-shelf advantage. If Celsius had the same shelf space as peers in every store, its share would be far higher. Amazon is an indicator of brick-and-mortar potential, which is why Celsius cites South Florida and other purchasable market data.
Closing thoughts on the international opportunity and anything to be aware of.

Monster is a benchmark (~37% of revenue international), but ~67% of Monster's ~$7.5B revenue is still US - underscoring the US must remain Celsius's focus. International is an incremental growth path, approached strategically without a 'shocking approach.' Canada entry announced for Q1 2024 with Pepsi Canada; evaluating Europe, Japan, Australia; Pepsi is the preferred (not mandated) international partner; build frameworks, execute in the first 12-18 months, then expand faster in 2025-2026.
